name: Create an enum and use it — customers and orders

customTypes.name: order_status
customTypes.comment: A closed, small set of states the application code already branches on. Read Gotchas before you reach for this on anything that grows.

customTypes.name: postal_address
customTypes.comment: A struct-shaped value with no lifecycle of its own — unlike order_status, nothing here ever needs a value added or removed.

tables.name: customers
tables.comment: One row per person who has ordered. mailing_address is a postal_address, typed by writing the type's name into the column's type cell.

columns.name: mailing_address
columns.comment: Composite type. Nullable: we only have it once an order ships.

tables.name: orders
tables.comment: status is an order_status, not a raw string — the column's type cell names the enum by name, same mechanism as mailing_address above.

columns.name: status
columns.comment: Every order starts pending. The quotes around pending are part of the default text you type.

notes.text:
Two kinds of custom type, two different lifecycles.

order_status is a closed set that PostgreSQL enforces for you. Adding a value later is ALTER TYPE order_status ADD VALUE 'returned' — cheap. Removing one is not: PostgreSQL has no DROP VALUE, so a value that turns out to be wrong means building a replacement type and migrating every column and default across. If a set of strings is going to grow or shrink over the table's life, a lookup table with a foreign key beats an enum every time.

postal_address has no such lifecycle problem — its shape is just documentation for a group of columns, not a constraint on their values.
